#### What this PR does / why we need it:
This PR makes improvements to queueset shuffle sharding and dispatching as well as further improvements to the queueset tests.

- Switch to a new anti-windup technique because the old one was too aggressive.  The new one's floor on a queue's next dispatch time is the arrival time of the request to be dispatched.
- When judging queues in the shuffle-sharding, look at seats in use as well as seats of waiting requests, because this is a more accurate reflection of how busy the queue is.
- In shuffle-sharding, do not always consider the items in the hand in the same order.  Before this change, I found that in scenarios with multiple flows going to the same queue, the flows got uneven treatment depending on the queue's position in each flow's hand.

With the above changes, we get better results.  This PR tightens the margins of several tests to reflect this.  This PR also makes some improvements in comments and private method names.

#### What happened:
I looked into why TestDifferentWidth in `queueset_test.go` needs surprisingly wide tolerance for divergence from the ideal result.  One reason is the anti-windup mechanism at https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b47f8263e18c7b13dba33fba23187e5e0477cdbd/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/flowcontrol/fairqueuing/queueset/queueset.go#L726-L742 is canceling the "credit" that the queues for the width=1 flow get from having requests wait in the queue.  For example, here is a bit of verbose logging from around the time the first round of requests finish and the second start (I am using a tweaked scenario, hoping a wider one will come closer to ideal --- it did not):

comments:
I started wondering what would happen if we would remove that completely:
- basically the virtual time of a particular queue can go arbitrarily into past, as long as there is always something in the queue (when at any point in time we empty the queue, the next incoming request will bring it back to "now")
- the queue may accumulate "credit" only if there is no request being currently processed from the queue (otherwise it's time is effectively advancing by at least its latency, potentially more for width>1)
- when choosing which queue to put a request to, we effectively don't use that time at all - we're only looking at the "number of waiting seats": https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dd2d12f6dc0e654c15d5db57a5f9f6ba61192726/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/flowcontrol/fairqueuing/queueset/queueset.go#L473


Given the first two points we definitely need some anti-windup mechanism, but I'm wondering what if instead of what we have now, (maxing with set virtual time), we would do:
`queue_virtual_time = max(queue_virtual_time, request_income_time)`

That is theoretically incorrect (even units don't match), but if we would change "request_income_time" to "virtual_time at the moment of request income" that makes more sense.
And that introduces some anti-windup protection.

@MikeSpreitzer - thoughts?
@wojtek-t : yes, that sounds plausible.  I will give it a try.

do we actually need an anti wind-up mechanism here? 

from dispatch - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/flowcontrol/fairqueuing/queueset/queueset.go#L696
```
currentVirtualFinish := queue.virtualStart + qs.estimatedServiceSeconds*float64(oldestWaiting.Seats())
```

so if `virtualStart` goes back into past, that queue is more likely to be selected for dispatch, right?

> so if virtualStart goes back into past, that queue is more likely to be selected for dispatch, right?

True, but if there are more requests than we're able to process, then each queue would be accumulating "credit" over time.
IN other words - I think we need some windup protection, but I have a feeling (no hard proof) that what i proposed above should be enough.

> the queue may accumulate "credit" only if there is no request being currently processed from the queue (otherwise it's time is effectively advancing by at least its latency, ...)

No, that's not exactly how windup happens.  Remember, a queue that is requesting less than it is allocated will be getting dispatched pretty well; if anything, requesting less than it is allocated risks the queue having no requests executing or queued at some moments --- after which the next arrival will catch up the queue's `virtualStart` (which is R(expected time of next dispatch in the virtual world)).

If such a queue manages to never be empty --- that is, always have requests executing or queued --- then the corrected advancement of the queue's `virtualStart` is slower than the advancement of the `virtualStart` of queues that are using more than they are allocated.  This difference is the credit/debit that we are talking about.  The existing anti-windup mechanism, and your suggested alternative, address one side of this coin: making the low-flow queues advance their `virtualStart` at least as fast as R is advancing.  But the other side of the coin, the even faster advancement of the `virtualStart` of the queues using more than they are allocated, remains unaddressed.

Following is a visualization of the existing queueset TestWindup.  You can see that in the first half of the test, during the windup, flow 1's queue (8) never goes empty --- it always has a request executing.  The dynamics of the queues are harder to see in this visualization; I am not pleased yet with the queue visualization.  For each request, its interval in the "Queues" columns is the time (remember real and virtual world use the same clock; R is a different thing, measuring progress in work) ranging from (a) the expected time of dispatch in the virtual world, as seen at the moment of dispatch in the real world, to (b) the real time corresponding to R((a) + the actual work of the request (i.e., width X observed duration)).  R(time (a)) = the queue's `virtualStart` just before dispatching the request.  You can see that for flow 1, the dispatches in the virtual world coincide with the dispatches in the real world during the first half of the test.  In contrast, for flow 0 the dispatches in the real world happen progressively more and more ahead of the dispatches in the virtual world in the first half of the test.  When flow 1's offered load doubles at the halfway point of the test, queue 8's `virtualStart` is about R(the current time) but queue 5's `virtualStart` (as seen by the dispatch of, e.g., request 0,1,20) is well ahead.  So flow 1 gets all it can take for a while, until around time 32 when both queues settle into real dispatches that anticipate virtual dispatches by about the same amount of time.

[windup.pdf](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/files/7193590/windup.pdf)

(In case it is not clear: this is not to disagree with the suggestion, only a bit of the analysis.)
